results.summary: This design consists of four inverters, where inputs zero to three pass directly to the corresponding outputs and the remaining inputs are inverted. It is intended to be exercised by toggling the input switches, requiring no external hardware. The documentation is very thin and partly garbled, so the exact mapping of the remaining input and output pins is not fully clear. It appears to be a simple logic experiment or class exercise rather than a complete functional block.

This project decodes a four-bit binary value into the seven-segment control signals needed to show the corresponding decimal digit. Inputs zero through three represent the binary number, and the outputs drive a common seven-segment display. It is tested by flipping the input switches and observing the displayed digit. No external hardware other than the display itself is required, and it is a straightforward educational decoder design.

This design is an eight-bit buffer that takes four-bit inputs and displays the loaded value. Switches seven and eight are used to load the upper four bits first and then the lower four bits. It is tested by playing with the switches to observe the loading behaviour. No external hardware is required, and the documentation describes it as a test workshop exercise.

This design lights the digit corresponding to whichever of the eight input switches is active, mapping switch one to digit one through switch eight to digit eight. It is tested by flipping individual switches and checking that the matching digit appears on the seven-segment display. External hardware includes an eight-switch array and a common-cathode seven-segment display. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the pin mapping and behaviour.

This design chains four flip-flops together and shifts the state of input in0 through them, driving a seven-segment display. It is tested by toggling the in0 switch and watching the shifted state appear on the display or LEDs. External hardware consists of a seven-segment display or LEDs plus a switch. The clock runs at 1 Hz, and the documentation is minimal but describes the shift behaviour.

This design displays the digit 1 on a seven-segment display whenever input IN0 is asserted. It is tested by wiring the outputs to a seven-segment display and turning on IN0. The only external hardware needed is a seven-segment display. The project is a minimal demonstration whose purpose is simply to show a fixed digit and is almost entirely without technical detail.

This project is described as a simple logic gate with two inputs and two outputs. The documentation only says 'Testing' for both how it works and how to test it, and it names no specific gate function. External hardware is listed vaguely as 'my hardware'. There is essentially no meaningful documentation, so the actual function cannot be determined.

This design claims that, after a very long delay, it will render the letter V, though the exact output encoding is not specified. It is tested by turning on input 1 and waiting. The external hardware section is left as the default placeholder text, giving no real information. The documentation is extremely thin and partly unreliable, so the design cannot be clearly characterised.

This design adds two four-bit binary numbers and drives the five-bit sum onto the outputs. Inputs zero through three carry number A and inputs four through seven carry number B, with the least significant bits at zero and four respectively; the output sum also has its least significant bit at output zero. It is tested by setting the switches for A and B and observing the LEDs. External hardware consists of eight input switches and five output LEDs, and the documentation is clear about the encoding despite being a simple class exercise.

This design checks whether the input value is odd or even and lights a green LED for odd and a red LED for even. It is tested by applying different input values and watching which LED illuminates. The documentation calls the inputs 'outputs' in the test description, but the intent is clear. No external hardware is required beyond the LEDs, and it is a simple educational parity detector.
